nameStory: Swamp agrimony gets its name from its preference for wetland habitats, unlike many of its relatives that thrive in drier places. The word 'agrimony' comes from the ancient Greek word 'argemone,' meaning 'healing to the eyes,' reflecting the long history of these plants in traditional medicine. It's also called 'harvestlice' because its burr-like fruits cling tenaciously to clothing and fur, just like unwanted hitchhikers!
description: Swamp agrimony is a perennial wildflower that belongs to the rose family, though you might not immediately recognize the family resemblance. This modest plant typically grows 2-4 feet tall with a somewhat sprawling habit. Like other agrimonies, it produces small yellow flowers arranged in slender spikes and has compound leaves that look almost fern-like from a distance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellow flowers, each about 1/4 inch across, bloom in narrow spikes at the top of stems. The flowers have five small petals and feel delicate when touched gently.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 5-9 toothed leaflets arranged in pairs along the stem, plus one at the tip. The leaflets feel slightly rough and have a fresh, green scent when crushed.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, hard burrs covered in hooked bristles that grab onto clothing and animal fur with remarkable tenacity. They make a slight scratching sound when pulled from fabric.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in loose colonies from creeping underground stems, creating patches rather than single isolated plants. Stems are often slightly reddish and feel firm but not woody.

habitat: True to its name, swamp agrimony prefers wet soils in marshes, swamp edges, wet meadows, and along stream banks throughout New England. It thrives in areas that stay consistently moist but aren't completely underwater, often growing alongside sedges, cattails, and other moisture-loving plants.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late spring with their distinctive compound pattern. Young growth has a fresh, bright green color.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from July through August, with small yellow flower spikes most visible during this time. The burr-like fruits begin forming by late summer.
seasonality.fall: Fruits are fully mature and at their stickiest, ready to hitch rides on passing animals and humans. Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only dried stems and scattered burrs as evidence of its presence.

funFact: Swamp agrimony is considered the most 'noxious' of all the agrimony species because its burrs are incredibly persistent - they can stay attached to clothing through multiple wash cycles and have been known to clog industrial wool-processing equipment!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other agrimony species, but swamp agrimony's preference for wet habitats is the key difference - if you find an agrimony in a marsh or swamp, it's probably this species. Remember: 'swamp agrimony loves swampy spots' while its cousins prefer drier ground.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the rose family, agrimonies look nothing like roses and lack thorns entirely. The family connection becomes clearer when you examine the five-petaled flowers closely under a magnifying glass, where you can see the same basic floral structure as their showier rose cousins.
compareHints: Swamp agrimony differs from tall hairy agrimony and roadside agrimony primarily by habitat - it's the wetland specialist of the group. While all agrimonies have similar yellow flowers and compound leaves, swamp agrimony tends to be less robust than tall hairy agrimony and grows in much wetter conditions than roadside agrimony, which prefers disturbed dry areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Tall hairy agrimony lives up to its name by being the tallest and fuzziest of New England's agrimonies.
Roadside agrimony differs from tall hairy agrimony by preferring sunnier, more disturbed sites rather than woodland edges.
Among New England's agrimonies, downy agrimony is distinguished by its exceptionally soft, velvety stem hairs and preference for drier sites.
